chapters.title: Overview: Ignite as a whole, and where the thin client sits

items.title: What Ignite is

phrases.text: This walk explains the Apache Ignite 2.17.0 thin client to an engineer who must debug it, in about twenty-two minutes plus the stops.
The README calls Ignite a distributed database for high-performance computing with in-memory speed.

code.anchor: distributed database for high-performance computing with in-memory speed

phrases.text: Its feature list includes distributed key-value storage, SQL, the structured query language, and compute and service grids.
Disk storage is optional: native persistence in a data region stays off unless you enable it.

items.title: Schema: Ignite at the top level

phrases.text: This schema, drawn from the 2.17.0 code, shows Ignite's server nodes and how clients reach them.
Nodes find each other through discovery. If you configure none, Ignite uses TcpDiscoverySpi.
Messages between nodes travel through the communication service, by default TcpCommunicationSpi.
A thick client is a full node in client mode; its discovery documentation says it routes discovery traffic through one server node.

code.anchor: use it as a router for discovery traffic.

phrases.text: Three kinds of remote clients share one server listener, the client connector: the thin client and the drivers for JDBC, Java Database Connectivity, and ODBC, Open Database Connectivity.

code.anchor: return new ClientConnectionContext(ctx, ses, connId, maxCursors, thinCfg);

phrases.text: REST, representational state transfer, over HTTP, the hypertext transfer protocol, starts only when the rest-http module is on the class path.

diagramFocus: Not a cluster node: it opens its own TCP
phrases.text: The thin client is not a node: it builds its own small network layer for TCP connections, transmission control protocol, to client connectors.
An application starts one with Ignition.startClient, which hands the configuration to TcpIgniteClient.

chapters.title: Preparations: version, build, layout and configuration

items.title: Version and build

phrases.text: The code is Apache Ignite 2.17.0, at the commit recorded with this walk; the parent build file sets the version, and Java 11 source level.
The developer notes give the full build through the Maven wrapper, mvnw: clean install with the all-java and licenses profiles, skipping tests.

action.where: a shell in the project root (Linux, WSL or macOS)
action.do:
./mvnw clean install -Pall-java,licenses -DskipTests
This is the full build from DEVNOTES.txt. The first run downloads Maven 3.8.3 (Maven wrapper) and all dependencies, so it needs network access and a JDK; the parent build file has profiles for JDK 11 to 14 and for 15 and later. The install also puts ignite-tools into the local Maven repository, which the surefire test plugin of this build needs for the test actions below. Not yet run.

./mvnw -pl modules/core test -DFORK_COUNT_SET_TO_1 -Dtest='FunctionalTest#testPutGet*'
FORK_COUNT_SET_TO_1 activates the profile that forks one test JVM, so the surefire argLine with the Java module options (java-11+ or java-15+ profile) applies. The quotes and the trailing star are needed because FunctionalTest is parameterized (useBinaryArrays), so its test names carry a suffix. items.title: Schema: where the code lives

phrases.text: This schema maps the thin-client code in the 2.17.0 source tree.
The public API, the application programming interface, is the package org.apache.ignite.client, starting with the IgniteClient interface.
The implementation is the internal package client.thin, led by TcpIgniteClient, which implements that interface.
On the server, the listener lives in the processors.odbc package; despite the name, it also serves JDBC and thin clients.
Thin-client specifics live in processors.platform.client: connection context, message parser, request handler, and the request classes.
FunctionalTest in the same module starts a server node and a client in one Java process, handy for debugging both sides.

items.title: Server configuration

phrases.text: Every server node starts a client connector by default: the node configuration holds a default connector configuration.
ClientConnectorConfiguration defaults: port 10800 with a range of 100, a ten-second handshake timeout, and an idle timeout of zero, meaning none.
It also turns thin clients, JDBC and ODBC on or off, all on by default, and holds the SSL, Secure Sockets Layer, settings.
ThinClientConfiguration sets limits: one hundred active transactions per connection, and zero compute tasks.
With zero, the server refuses thin-client compute with a functionality disabled error.

code.anchor: Compute grid functionality is disabled for thin clients on server node.

items.title: Client configuration

phrases.text: On the client, an address without a port expands to every port from 10800 to 10900.
Each port is a separate endpoint, so one address without a port gives a hundred and one endpoints.
The timeout defaults to zero, which means wait without limit.
Partition awareness and cluster discovery are on, reconnects are throttled to three per thirty seconds, and the retry policy agrees to every retry.
Heartbeats are off by default.

chapters.title: Main design ideas of the thin client

items.title: Idea one, with a schema: a binary protocol over TCP

phrases.text: This schema shows the protocol frames as the 2.17.0 code writes and reads them.
Design idea one: a binary protocol over TCP. Every message starts with a four-byte length that does not count itself.
Numbers are little-endian, whatever the machine.
A request then holds a two-byte operation code, an eight-byte request id, and the payload.

diagramFocus: byte flags: 1 keep binary, 2 transaction, 4 expiry
phrases.text: A cache payload starts with the cache id and a flags byte; expiry durations, then a transaction id, follow only when flagged.

diagramFocus: int16 flags (1.4.0+): 1 error, 2 topology changed, 4 notification
phrases.text: A response starts with the request id. From protocol version 1.4.0, two bytes of flags follow: error, topology changed, and notification.
With the topology flag, the new topology version follows; with the error flag, a status code and a message follow.
The first message must be a handshake of at most 64 mebibytes, whose first three bytes are the handshake code and major version one or two.

items.title: Idea two: versions and features agreed per connection

phrases.text: Design idea two: version and features are agreed per connection. The client proposes protocol version 1.7.0 and can fall back to 1.0.0.

code.anchor: private static final ProtocolVersion DEFAULT_VERSION = LATEST_VER;

phrases.text: The handshake carries the version, client type two, the client's feature bitmask, user attributes, and the user name and password if set.
The reply carries the agreed features and, from 1.4.0, the server's node id.
If the server refuses the version, it names its own; the client retries with it if supported, and otherwise fails.
A wrong password makes the handshake throw a client authentication exception.
It is not a connection error, so the call tries no other server.

items.title: Idea three: many requests on one connection

phrases.text: Design idea three: requests share a connection. Each channel numbers requests from one and keeps the pending ones by id.

code.anchor: private final AtomicLong reqId = new AtomicLong(1);

phrases.text: On the server, each message goes to a thread pool, so requests from one connection can finish out of order.
A synchronous call waits on its future, with the configured timeout when it is above zero.
If that timeout fires, the call fails with a plain client exception, and nothing tells the server to stop.
So a timed-out put may still be applied, and its late reply goes unused.
The reliable channel retries only connection exceptions, so the call is not retried, and the connection stays open.
An asynchronous call only registers a listener, so the wait for its response has no client-side timeout.
The same timeout setting limits two more waits of every new channel: first, the socket connect.
Second, the handshake reply. A handshake timeout is a connection error, so, unlike a request timeout, the call can move to another server.

items.title: Ideas four to six: partition awareness, failover, security

phrases.text: Design idea four: partition awareness. With a current partition map, a key operation goes straight to the node the map names; otherwise the reliable channel picks one.
Design idea five: failover. After a connection error the call moves to another server, while attempts remain and the retry policy agrees.
Design idea six: security is optional. The server authenticates a client only when security is enabled on the node.
The handshake sends the user name and password as plain strings: without SSL they cross the network in clear text.
On the client, SSL stays off until you set an SSL mode other than disabled.
On the server, sslEnabled adds an SSL filter, by default with the node's SSL context factory; sslClientAuth demands client certificates.
A security exception in a request reaches the client as a client authorization exception.

items.title: What a thin client does not offer

phrases.text: Compared with the Ignite interface, IgniteClient has no data streamer, events, messaging, locks, latches, semaphores, queues or atomic sequences; it does offer atomic longs and sets.

code.anchor: public ClientAtomicLong atomicLong(String name, long initVal, boolean create);

phrases.text: Compute takes a task name, not code, so the task class must already be on the servers.

code.anchor: public <T, R> R execute(String taskName, @Nullable T arg)

chapters.title: Modules: the client side and the server side

items.title: Schema: the client side

phrases.text: This schema shows the client-side classes of 2.17.0 in call order.
TcpIgniteClient is the facade; its constructor builds the binary marshaller and the reliable channel, then connects.
TcpClientCache is a light handle: asking the client for a cache by name sends nothing to the server.

code.anchor: return new TcpClientCache<>(name, ch, marsh, transactions, lsnrsRegistry);

phrases.text: So a wrong cache name fails only at the first operation, when the server says the cache does not exist.
TcpClientChannel is one TCP connection: it holds the socket, numbers the requests and keeps their futures until the responses arrive.
All channels of one client share one multiplexer, a GridNioServer in client mode with a single selector.
When the client writes a binary type it has not registered yet, or whose metadata has changed, it first sends a separate put binary type request.

items.title: Schema: the server side

phrases.text: This schema shows the server side in 2.17.0, from the socket to the cache and back.
ClientListenerProcessor starts a GridNioServer named client-listener, with the connector's selector count.
Incoming bytes pass the SSL filter if SSL is on, then the codec filter, which builds one client message per frame.
Then the async notify filter hands each message to the processor's executor.
That executor is the client-connector pool, sized by the connector's thread pool size, with an unbounded queue.
ClientListenerNioListener receives it: with no connection context yet, it is the handshake; afterwards, a request to decode and handle.
ClientRequestHandler runs a request directly or, if it is asynchronous, waits briefly and otherwise answers when its future completes.
Cache key requests are asynchronous only on transactional caches; the code comment says such operations can block the thread.
Cache key requests, such as put and get, use the server's cache in keep-binary mode, so keys and values stay binary there.
When a client disconnects, the server cleans up its resources.
It also closes the client's open transactions.

chapters.title: Top-level workflows: connect, put and get, routing and failover

items.title: Workflow a: connect and handshake

phrases.text: This sequence, drawn from the 2.17.0 code, shows the connect and the handshake.
channelsInit takes its endpoints from the discovery context; before any discovery, those are the configured addresses.

code.anchor: String[] hostAddrs = addrFinder == null ? addresses : addrFinder.getAddresses();

phrases.text: The reliable channel keeps its channels in holders of the ClientChannelHolder class: each holds a group of addresses, the channel to them, and the times of its reconnect attempts.
One holder is the default, the one connected first; at start it is picked at random among the holders with the lowest port.
Then it connects the default holder: a new TcpClientChannel tries the holder's addresses in turn until a socket opens.
On the server, each new connection gets a handshake timer, ten seconds by default; without a handshake in time, the session closes with a warning.

code.anchor: Unable to perform handshake within timeout

phrases.text: The server reads the version and client type, builds the connection context, and checks the type is enabled and the version supported.
initializeFromHandshake reads the features, attributes and credentials, authenticates, and creates the request handler and message parser.
On success the server cancels the timer and replies true, its features and node id; on failure, false, a version, a message and a status.
The holder then registers the reliable channel as a topology listener, and files the channel under the server's node id.
With partition awareness on, channelsInit then starts connecting all other holders in the background.
That task ignores the reconnect throttle: an address without a port can cost a hundred and one connect attempts, each failure a warning with a logger set.
The server flags the first response on each connection as topology changed, since it has reported no version there yet.
That reaches onTopologyChanged, which, in the background, refreshes the server endpoints and, with partition awareness, runs channelsInit again.

items.title: Debugging the connect: breakpoints and logs

phrases.text: To watch this, debug the put and get functional test, starting at TcpClientChannel.handshake and ClientListenerNioListener.onHandshake; the action lists the rest.

code.anchor: private void handshake(ProtocolVersion ver, String user, String pwd, Map<String, String> userAttrs)

phrases.text: On the server, a refused version, client type or recovery mode logs the warning error during handshake; a wrong password only logs client authentication failed, at debug level.

action.where: the server node started by the node action

If the node logs through java.util.logging (Ignite's fallback when the log4j2 module is not on the class path), add to config/java.util.logging.properties of the node and restart it:

The client connections system view lists each node's open client connections, and the control script can print it.

items.title: Workflow b: a cache put and a cache get

phrases.text: This sequence, drawn from the 2.17.0 code, follows a put and a get from the client API to the cache and back.
ClientCache put rejects a null key or value, then runs a single-key operation with the cache put code.
Outside a transaction, a keyed call goes to affinityService on the reliable channel; inside one, to the transaction's own channel.

code.anchor: return ch.affinityService(cacheId, affKey, op, payloadWriter, payloadReader);

phrases.text: The chosen channel's send takes the next request id, registers a future under it, and writes the frame to the session.
On the server, a client-connector thread decodes the frame and, for the put code, builds a ClientCachePutRequest.
For an atomic cache the request runs on this thread and calls put on the server's IgniteCache; this walk stops there.
Before that, outside transactions, it counts whether this node is primary for the key, on partitioned caches with statistics on: a check of partition awareness.
The put answers with just a header: with flags in use and no error, the request id and flags, plus the topology version when the topology flag is set.

code.anchor: If no return flag is set, no additional data is written to a payload.

phrases.text: On the client's selector thread, processNextMessage matches the id, removes the pending future and completes it, waking the caller.
get takes the same path with the cache get code, and no value in the request.
On the server, ClientCacheGetRequest calls get and wraps the value in a ClientObjectResponse.
The client then deserializes the value, unless the cache handle keeps binary.

items.title: Errors on the put path: breakpoints and logs

phrases.text: If processing throws, the server logs failed to process client request, and sends back a status code and a message.
It adds the server's stack trace only when configured to, which is off by default.
On the client, the error arrives as a ClientServerError with that status code, as the cause of a ClientException.
Breakpoints for this path: TcpClientCache.put on the client and ClientCachePutRequest.process0 on the server; the action lists the rest.

items.title: Workflow c: choosing the node for a key, and failover

phrases.text: This sequence, drawn from the 2.17.0 code, shows how a key finds its node, and what happens when a node is lost.
If the cache's mapping is missing or older than the last topology, one thread at a time refetches it in its own call; others go without. With no last topology yet, nothing is fetched.
The server maps only partitioned caches with the default rendezvous affinity and no custom key mapper, unless custom mappings are requested.

code.anchor: Only RendezvousAffinityFunction is supported for now.

phrases.text: To place a key, the client converts it to binary and takes its affinity key field, if its type has one configured.
The default mapper computes the partition with the rendezvous formula, and the map turns the partition into a primary node id.
The mapping is used only while a channel to at least one node of the last topology is open.
With a node id, the reliable channel uses that node's channel; without one, it chooses a channel as for any other call.
In a synchronous call, if the node's channel fails, the client records it and, unless one attempt is the limit, asks the retry policy before trying another channel.
When a server goes away, its channel closes, and every pending request fails with a connection exception: channel is closed.
The reliable channel catches only connection exceptions.
For each, it logs channel failure, closes the channel, runs the fail listeners and, if its holder was the default, moves the default on.
Then the policy decides: system operations, with no public type, are always retried; public ones only if the policy agrees.
The default policy agrees to everything, writes included: a put whose connection broke may already be applied, and is sent again on the next attempt, if one remains.
To limit that, ClientRetryReadPolicy agrees only for reads.
ClientRetryNonePolicy never agrees; one repeat, described shortly, can still happen before any policy is asked.

diagramFocus: attempts = holders, or retryLimit if smaller and above 0;
phrases.text: The number of attempts is the number of holders, or the retry limit when that is above zero and smaller.

diagramFocus: one more with partition awareness and more than one open channel
phrases.text: With partition awareness on and several channels open, the first try goes to a random open channel, with one extra attempt.
When the number of failures equals the number of attempts, not counting the extra one, and no channel is open, the client resets discovery to the configured addresses and rebuilds its holders.

One path differs: in a synchronous call with partition awareness on, if a channel that was already open turns out broken, it is reconnected and the call repeated once; only a further failure reaches the policy.

code.anchor: same channel and repeat the operation.

phrases.text: Asynchronous calls have no such repeat, and when they cannot connect, they move on to another channel without asking the policy.

code.anchor: channel -> applyOnClientChannelAsync(fut, channel, op, payloadWriter, payloadReader, failures),

phrases.text: Transactions do not fail over: their operations use the transaction's channel, where a connection error ends with transaction context has been lost.

code.anchor: Transaction context has been lost due to connection errors.

items.title: Notes

phrases.text: Some notes. The client's tcpNoDelay setting is copied into each channel's configuration, but never used.
The client's network layer always turns TCP no-delay on.
Flow control is loose: the client sets no limit on pending requests.

code.anchor: private final Map<Long, ClientRequestFuture> pendingReqs = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

phrases.text: On the server, only the optional session outbound queue limit, off by default, disconnects a client that reads too slowly.
Once a session's outbound queue reaches that limit, the server closes the session and, when the close succeeds, logs a warning.
The server's idle timeout is off by default; when set, idle sessions are closed, so clients then need heartbeats.
Durability, replication and consistency come from the cache, not the thin client: the put response follows the server's cache call.
The thin client's main sources carry no to-do or fix-me markers on either side; one test has a to-do.

items.title: Open questions and limits of this walk

phrases.text: With heartbeats on and supported by the server, the channel's constructor sets them up.
That first asks the server for its idle timeout, and waits for the reply.
Only after the constructor returns does the reliable channel register as the channel's topology listener.
The server, though, marks that first reply with the topology flag, because the connection has no last topology version yet, so the flag reaches no listener.

By the code, partition awareness then has no last topology, and fetches no partition map until a later response reports a newer topology version; whether this happens in practice is an open question, not yet tested.
A note on channelsInit: its endpoint branch runs only when no channel is open right after the default one connected, so a normal start skips it.
Not covered: the JDBC, ODBC and other language clients; timings and real failover need a running cluster.
